plan.topic: Do GLP-1 medicines slow biological aging? Aging-clock data reported by drugmakers (CNN Oct 13, MIT Technology Review Oct 6)
plan.angle: Title: 'Do Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) or Semaglutide (Ozempic) Slow Aging? What's Actually Shown #shorts'. Within 10 s: 'Not shown yet. These are early aging-clock readings the drugmakers presented, in people with overweight, obesity or diabetes. They're not a lifespan result.' Aging clock = blood or protein markers that estimate 'biological age', not years lived. Experts say these clocks are still in development. Figure: 'Novo Nordisk told MIT Technology Review the difference vs placebo was around 2 to 3 years, depending on the clock and organ.' Caveat: 'Lilly told CNN the effects are mostly due to blood-sugar and weight changes.' Expert line: 'An aging researcher told CNN it's too early to take these drugs just to live longer.' What IS shown: SELECT (fewer heart attacks, strokes and CV deaths in adults with heart disease and overweight/obesity, without diabetes) and FLOW (kidney outcomes in adults with T2D and chronic kidney disease). One line on common GI side effects. No #antiaging, #longevity or brand hashtags. Close with 'talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you'.
plan.working_title: Does Mounjaro or Ozempic Slow Aging? What the Data Actually Shows #shorts
plan.why:
A rising topic (momentum 80) as a 'what does it do to my body?' question with named drugs. It rebuilds the Oct 13 carousel as a Short, as the playbook asks. | fact-check: The topic is legitimate and the planned framing is cautious. However, the figure and its attribution are wrong.
- MIT Technology Review (Oct 6, 2026) quotes Novo's Nikolaj Roed: overall difference 'around two to three years'.
- CNN (Oct 13) reports Novo researchers saying semaglutide lowered the heart's biological age by 2–4 years vs placebo, and other organs by 1–4 years.
So the '2–3 years, as CNN reported' credit is wrong.
The weight-loss caveat is split:
- Lilly's Kevin Duffin told CNN the effects are 'mostly due to' blood-sugar reduction and weight loss.
- Novo said its effects were 'not completely explained by weight loss'.
Use both. Do not claim one caveat applies to all the data.
CNN's caution comes from Dr. James Kirkland: 'people could overread some of this stuff'. He says it's too early to use these drugs solely to live longer, and that clocks 'are still in development' and 'vary tremendously from day to day'.
These are exploratory, company-presented biomarker data (ARDD 2026 meeting), not peer-reviewed lifespan outcomes. Keep that hedge.
Risk: the topic can encourage off-label 'anti-aging' use in people without obesity or diabetes. Say explicitly that it was studied in people with overweight/obesity or diabetes.
The title with two brands leans toward an ad. Lead with generics.
Populations for the proven benefits: SELECT and FLOW as listed in the angle are correct.

social.facebook_caption:
You've probably seen headlines saying GLP-1 medicines might slow aging. Here's the real story: that's not shown yet.

The aging-clock data is company-reported (Novo Nordisk and Lilly), not peer-reviewed, and it comes from people who already had overweight, obesity or diabetes. These "clocks" estimate biological age — they don't measure lifespan. A Cedars-Sinai researcher told CNN people could overread this, and that the clocks are still in development. What's actually well-established: semaglutide reduced combined heart attacks, strokes or heart deaths in adults with heart disease and overweight/obesity, without diabetes (SELECT trial), and reduced major kidney events in people with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease (FLOW trial). Common side effects include nausea, diarrhea and constipation.

factcheck.summary: The Short is accurate and well hedged, but it needs one attribution fix before it can pass. I checked it against MIT Technology Review (Oct 6, 2026) and the CNN article (Oct 13, 2026). I couldn't open the CNN URL directly (HTTP 451), so I read its syndicated copy on KEYT. Both sources back the ~2–3 year Novo protein-clock figure, Novo's placebo comparison, Lilly's line that the effects are "mostly due to" blood-sugar reduction and weight loss, Novo's "not completely explained by weight loss, blood sugar control or inflammation", and Kirkland's quotes. The problem: "no placebo group" is CNN's own description of Lilly's SURMOUNT-5-based analysis. Lilly didn't say it, but s4 makes it sound like Lilly told CNN. Crediting a claim to the wrong source is a recurring reason we hold pieces. Two smaller wording issues: Novo's data is a preprint ahead of peer review, so "not yet peer-reviewed" fits better than "not peer-reviewed". And the "too early" line came from Kirkland alone, not from several experts. The SELECT and FLOW populations are stated correctly. The side effects match STEP 1 and SURMOUNT-1. The prescriber line is in both s8 and the CTA. There's no dosing, no medication-change advice and no gray-market sources. The script is about 150 words, under the 170-word limit.

issues.claim: Lilly told CNN effects were mostly due to blood-sugar reduction and weight loss, with no placebo group.
issues.problem: The wording credits 'no placebo group' to Lilly. In the CNN article, that is the reporter's own description: 'There was no placebo group who were not using any weight loss meds to compare against the people on tirzepatide… and the follow-up was relatively brief.' Lilly's analysis used SURMOUNT-5, which compared tirzepatide with semaglutide.
issues.fix: Lilly told CNN the effects were mostly due to blood-sugar reduction and weight loss. CNN notes Lilly's data had no placebo group. Novo said its results weren't completely explained by weight loss, blood sugar or inflammation. Early company data, not yet peer-reviewed.

issues.problem: CNN says Novo's study was posted as a preprint ahead of peer review, and Lilly's data was presented at a conference. 'Not peer-reviewed' sounds final. 'Not yet peer-reviewed' is accurate.
issues.fix: on_screen_text: "Company data, not yet peer-reviewed"; visual.fact: "Early company-presented aging-clock data (preprint/conference), not yet peer-reviewed; no lifespan results"

issues.claim: Experts say it's too early to take these drugs just to live longer.
issues.problem: CNN gives this line to Kirkland alone, not to several experts.
issues.fix: He added it's too early to take these drugs just in the hope of living longer.

issues.claim: Novo Nordisk reported semaglutide users' protein-clock biological age was around 2 to 3 years lower than placebo.
issues.problem: This is accurate (MIT: 'two to three years', varying by clock and organ). To keep the scope exact, say it was an average across clocks.
issues.fix: Novo Nordisk reported semaglutide users' protein-clock biological age was around 2 to 3 years lower than placebo, depending on the clock.

issues.claim: SELECT: fewer combined heart attacks, strokes or heart deaths on semaglutide
issues.problem: The claim is correct, but it has no number. Our house rule pairs every benefit with its absolute rates. This is optional, and it's fine to cut if word count matters.
issues.fix: Shown: SELECT: 20% fewer combined heart attacks, strokes or heart deaths on semaglutide (6.5% vs 8.0% on placebo, about 3 years), in adults with heart disease and overweight or obesity, without diabetes.

hold_reason: Dropped by Editor-in-Chief: The major attribution error the fact-checker flagged is still there. The script's s4 and the Instagram caption both say "Lilly told CNN … with no placebo group", but that was CNN's own description, not Lilly's, so the claim is credited to a source that never said it. Separately, the subtitle check shows the script text reads "c meglutide" where the narrator says "semaglutide", which suggests a phonetic misspelling in the on-screen captions. Both need fixing and a re-render before this can go out.

audio.soundNotes: Music sits well already (−13.5 dB under voice, −14.1 in pauses), so gain stays at 1.0; no need to push louder. The main issue was SFX density and a few hot spots: trimmed duplicate/simultaneous stock sounds in six busy clusters (6.9–8.6s, 12.3–13.1s, 30.6–31.1s, 63.4–65s, 76.3–78s, 81.1–81.6s) down to 3–4 per second, and pulled down several cues that read too loud over narration — especially the two blips at 77.1s/77.6s which were almost as loud as the voice (−6.7/−7.2 dB) and now sit at a felt −16 dB. Added four bespoke, topic-specific accents (aging-clock tick, SELECT heartbeat, FLOW water trickle, warm closing chime) to make the key reveals feel bespoke rather than generic pops.

issues.claim: Shown: SELECT heart benefit (heart disease + overweight/obesity, no diabetes), FLOW kidney benefit (T2D + CKD).
issues.problem: The post never says these benefits were for semaglutide. Since it opens with "GLP-1s", a reader could take the heart and kidney benefits as true of every GLP-1, tirzepatide included. That's broader than the script, which says "on semaglutide".
issues.fix: "GLP-1s slow aging"? Not shown yet: aging-clock data is company-reported, not peer-reviewed. Shown for semaglutide: SELECT heart benefit (heart disease + overweight/obesity, no diabetes), FLOW kidney benefit (T2D + CKD). Common side effects: nausea, diarrhea, constipation.
